_comment: Filter lists AdGuard Home should have enabled, applied by adguard/apply-filters.py.
This file is the source of truth; the running instance is reconciled to it.
Chosen for ONE job above all: killing the advertising SDKs embedded in Android
games running in the Google Play Games crosvm VM. The generic 'AdGuard DNS filter'
alone left roughly 20% of in-game ads getting through.
Deliberately NOT included: HaGeZi Pro++/Ultimate and 1Hosts Xtra. They block more,
but they over-block, and a game that will not start is a worse outcome than an ad -
it turns the parent against the whole system.

filters.name: AdGuard DNS filter
filters.why: Baseline: AdGuard Base + Social + Tracking + Mobile Ads + EasyList/EasyPrivacy.

filters.name: AWAvenue Ads Rule
filters.why: THE list for this problem. Targets advertising SDKs inside Android apps specifically, which is exactly what the games embed.

filters.name: AdAway Default Blocklist
filters.why: Android hosts list. Was already present in AdGuard but shipped DISABLED, which is easy to miss.

filters.name: Dandelion Sprout's Game Console Adblock List
filters.why: Ad endpoints specific to games rather than the web.

filters.name: HaGeZi's Pro Blocklist
filters.why: Broad ads/tracking/telemetry. 'Pro', not Pro++ or Ultimate: those over-block and start breaking the games themselves.

filters.name: Peter Lowe's Blocklist
filters.why: Small, old, very low false-positive rate. Cheap insurance.

_deliberately_not_enabled_comment: apply-filters.py reads only 'filters', so anything parked here stays off. It lives
in this file rather than nowhere because a list that is merely absent gets re-added
by the next person who thinks it looks useful; a list with a recorded reason does
not. These two were enabled by mistake on 2026-08-19 and turned back off the same
day at the parent's call - see the 'why' on each.

deliberately_not_enabled.name: HaGeZi's Encrypted DNS/VPN/TOR/Proxy Bypass
deliberately_not_enabled.why: OFF at the parent's decision, 2026-08-19. It does close a real hole - a browser with its own DoH resolver ignores this whole stack, which is how Avast Secure DNS and Opera GX's VPN got around it before - but it blocks dns.google, cloudflare-dns.com and the rest, and any device on this network that is configured to use DoH loses name resolution entirely rather than degrading. On a family network that reads as 'the internet is broken'. Re-enable only together with checking no phone or TV here is set to a Private DNS / secure-DNS provider.
deliberately_not_enabled.tradeoff: While this is off, the YouTube block is bypassable by any browser that ships its own DoH. The Windows machine-policy lane (safehouse_setup/browser.py sets DnsOverHttpsMode=off) is what covers that gap on the PC; nothing covers it on a phone or tablet.

deliberately_not_enabled.name: HaGeZi's Threat Intelligence Feeds
deliberately_not_enabled.why: OFF at the parent's decision, 2026-08-19. Two million rules of malware/phishing/scam blocking, and the same over-blocking objection as Pro++/Ultimate above applies at ten times the size: the failure mode is a game or a site that simply will not load, with no obvious cause and nothing in the UI pointing at this list.

known_false_positives.blocked_by: the GoodbyeAds adlist, via Pi-hole - not by any list in this file
known_false_positives.impact: Firebase app-instance registration: the identity call an Android app makes at startup. Blocking it removes no advertising at all, and its failure mode is a game that will not launch or will not sign in - so once the standing policy became 'the games must keep working' there was nothing left arguing for the block.
known_false_positives.how: Allowed in BOTH resolvers, because either one alone still answers 0.0.0.0: '@@||firebaseinstallations.googleapis.com^' in adguard/user-rules.txt, and the same host in blocklists/allowlist.txt which scripts/load-blocklists.sh loads into Pi-hole as an exact allow (type 0).
